title: Silent Film Comedy and American Culture
abstract: Alan Bilton's Silent Film Comedy and American Culture brings to mind Robert Allen and Douglas Gomery's observation that film history is not a simple empiricist history. They quote the American historian Charles Beard to remind us that, at best, film history must always remain a subjective ideological history: “Whatever acts of purification the historian may perform he yet remains human, a creature of time, place, circumstance, interests, predilections, culture.”1 Allen and Gomery divide the field of film history into four major areas, representing the major avenues of film historical investigation: Aesthetic film history deals with the history of the cinema as an art form; Technological film history involves the study of the origins and development of the technology that makes possible the creation and presentation of movies; Economic film history concerns who pays for movies and how and why they are made; Social film history is concerned principally with three questions: (1) Who made films and why? (2) Who saw films, how, and why? (3) What was seen, how and, why?2 The title of Bilton's first chapter is “Introducing America's Silent Film Comedy: Clowns, Conformity, Consumerism” and confirms what the title of his book already suggested, namely that Bilton adheres mostly to the social approach to film history with some minor attention to the economic approach. This selective approach is perhaps the book's strongest aspect and its greatest weakness in that it avoids a whole set of questions concerning the aesthetic and technological categories of film history.In his analysis of the relationship between silent comedies and the development of practical capitalism and consumerism in the U.S. during the turn of the twentieth century, Bilton relies heavily on the work of Sigmund Freud's nephew, Edward Bernays, who was one of Hoover's key speechwriters, as well as one of the most important architects of Western consumer culture. Bilton proposes that slapstick movies, with their use of destruction, comically uninhibited lust, illogical gags, and absurdist anarchy, provide a test case for Bernays's theories, which for the first time applied psychoanalysis to explain economic and cultural phenomena. Bilton aims to explore whether such manic energies can be absorbed and tamed by the system, or whether instead they illuminate the essential irrationality of consumer culture and the transformation of civic duty into boundless desire. Bilton quotes Rob King's study of the Keystone Film Company, which states that the “timeless” age of silent comedy can only be understood in terms of “a shift from a producer to a consumer economy” (29). Thus, Bilton claims that one should read all slapstick comedy as a form of collective anxiety dream.Bilton raises the important paradox of slapstick: on the one hand, it serves as a subversive tool that attacks social norms, while on the other hand, as comedy, it serves an essentially conservative purpose, restraining excessive activity by redirecting its energy to humor and laughter. This issue is very crucial to all humor study and is probably one of the preeminent unsolved questions regarding humor and its effects on society and politics. Analyzing Keaton and Chaplin's films, which are rich in satirical and subversive gags, could suggest a broader approach to this issue and might expose the dichotomy, which leads to the above-mentioned paradox as an oversimplified attitude. The context of the gag may be the key to understanding whether it is subversive or submissive.Bilton's narrow focus on the social perspective enables him to encapsulate the entire oeuvre of the seven most iconic and popular silent comedians: Mack Sennett, Charlie Chaplin, Rosco “Fatty” Arbuckle, Mabel Normand, Harold Lloyd, Buster Keaton, and Harry Langdon. He observes that Sennett's movies should be read “not as absurd Dada provocation, but rather as a cock-eyed reflection of the immigrant experience, its kicks, knocks and scums” (48). Or as he sums it up: “If the key theme of a Demille picture is the Cinderella theme, Sennett's films remain stubbornly ugly sisters: grimy, grotty, redolent of the dirt under the audience's fingernails that Demille was so committed to scrubbing out” (59).For Bilton, Chaplin is the ultimate seismograph of time (i.e., zeitgeist) of the mechanical era and is defined as “the exemplar of a nascent machine-body for a new machine-age” (99). Bilton supports his argument using Fernand Léger's iconic image of Chaplin in his short avant-garde film La Ballet Mechanique (1924) where the Tramp is transformed into jerky cubist animation, when the bodily and the mechanical become virtually inseparable. Along these lines, Roscoe “Fatty” Arbuckle is described as the “perfect representative of an age of gluttony and conspicuous consumption, the ravenous hunger of the market place” (114). Chaplin's most common props and sets are machines and their derivatives (statues, models, mannequins, toys, etc.), to the point that the border between people and objects is erased; meanwhile, Arbuckle's most reliable prop is food.One of the more interesting points of Bilton's analysis occurs when he applies his approach to Mabel Normand and the notion of the female clown. Through her films, Bilton explores the theoretical idea of the changing role of the New Woman in the early part of the twentieth century: “‘woman as sign’ and ‘woman as a token of exchange’”(139).Bilton tries to encapsulate Harold Lloyd's comedy as the ultimate expression of the anxieties of capitalism by focusing on one of his best achievements, Safety Last (1923). Bilton notes that the fact that Harold's character is a department store salesperson underscores the role of consumerism. Here he misses an opportunity to explore this theme and film against Chaplin's Modern Times (1936), and Keaton's Cops (1922) and One Week (1920). Such a comparative analysis could enhance his argument and show the uniqueness of each of these artists.Bilton writes that “it is Buster Keaton who most completely inhabits and exemplifies the machine age…. No other comedian of the period seems so aware of the essentially mechanical nature of the medium, its specifically machine-made possibilities and absurdities” (175). This observation is productive and accurate; however, failing to compare Keaton to Chaplin from this perspective in order to fully understand the meaning of this statement and the specialty of each of the two artists is another missed opportunity. Chaplin's work, especially the unique and sophisticated way he dealt with sound, was very much a result of his awareness of the mechanical nature of the medium.3Bilton quotes Gilbert Adair regarding the equivocal experience of watching a silent film today: “On the one hand the images feel incredibly young, with film-makers working out the possibilities of the medium for the very first time. On the other hand, however, the images appear incredibly, ineffably old” (192). Bilton suggests that of all of the great auteurs of the dead language of silent film, Keaton seems to have understood this duality most clearly. I believe that awareness of this tension between primitive, vital new medium and vanishing dying medium could provide important insight into many silent films toward the late 1920s, as the medium reached its climax.Bilton ends his survey by focusing on Harry Langdon and his “repetition-compulsion” about World War I. Using Jean Laplanche's concept of afterwardness, Bilton raises the apparent paradox of portraying World War I as comedy and describes how deferred meanings or effects can be understood to be activated only by a second occurrence of meaningful events. He argues that what in many ways distinguished Langdon's silent comedies was his ability to reveal the war's absurdity by revisiting the trenches and the expressions of the shell-shocked.In conclusion, Bilton's social approach highlights some aspects relevant for cultural studies and is particularly valuable for its contribution to humor studies. This approach allows Bilton to focus on a number of themes relevant to the social changes and developments of American society at the beginning of the twentieth century; what is more, it allows him to explore the reflection of these themes and their influence on the silent comedy and its major artists. I believe that incorporating other approaches, such as the aesthetic, technological, and economic, could enrich this analysis.Bilton's choice to focus on seven comedians and to structure the book around this idea implies a hidden assumption of what constitutes an auteur-oriented approach. There is no reference or treatment of the differences between these auteurs. Are these artists all equally auteurs? Are the differences between them only thematic or is there more that differentiates them than simply their gender and their external form/appearance? What does it mean for them to be comedians? Are we dealing with them just as clowns or actors? Or maybe one should also refer to the fact that some of them were only performers and others also writers, directors, and producers? Writing about cinema should relate to many aspects of the process of filmmaking. It is impossible to focus only on one of the categorizations that Allen and Gomery suggest. In spite of these flaws, the book gives an interesting overview and provides some insights into slapstick, one of silent cinema's greatest and most popular art forms; indeed, slapstick has proven to be an important contribution of American culture to the art of cinema, and remains as one of the greatest contributions of American cinema to today's culture.

title: ERJAVEC ALEŠ, ed. Aesthetic Revolutions and Twentieth-Century Avant-Garde Movements. Duke University Press, 2015, xvi + 322 pp., 70 b&w illus., $99.95 cloth.
abstract: In his introduction, Aleš Erjavec lays out the central thesis of the volume: that select avant‐garde movements of the twentieth century offer not only radical changes in artistic style and technique, but also aim toward transforming the destiny of the human world. Central to Erjavec's thesis are two key concepts: “aesthetic avant‐garde” and “aesthetic revolution.” The discussion begins with a proposed distinction between “aesthetic avant‐garde” and “artistic avant‐garde” movements. Aesthetic avant‐garde movements (i.e., futurism) aim to transform the world by initiating or contributing to revolutionary social and political programs. Artistic avant‐garde movements (i.e., cubism) are concerned with innovation and change in artistic styles and techniques relating to different stages in the history of art. Aesthetic revolution—the other major conceptual construct in the framing of Erjavec's thesis—refers to the projected or actual outcomes that result from the historical unfoldings of the respective aesthetic avant‐garde movements which are, in part, grounded in the views concerning the relation of aesthetics and politics that can be found in the writings of Friedrich Schiller and Jacques Rancière. By linking aesthetic revolutions and avant‐garde art movements together in the same volume, Erjavec, editor and contributor, draws attention to powerful motivations for change and innovation within aesthetics and the arts as they strive to influence social and political realities in the world. In addition to his own essays, which form the introduction and the conclusion, this volume includes essays on futurism (Sascha Bru), constructivism (John E. Bowlt), surrealism (Raymond Spiteri), modern Latin American avant‐garde and revolutionary movements (David Craven), the aesthetic revolution in the United States during the 1960s (Tyrus Miller), the situationist aesthetic revolution (Raymond Spiteri), and NSK—a Slovenian artistic activism movement (Miško Šuvaković). The authors’ writings exemplify the general thesis of the volume by offering seven different instances of the aesthetic avant‐garde movement in different cultural contexts. Sascha Bru's essay, “Politics and the Art of the Impossible,” cites Italian futurism as the model for future avant‐garde movements and, arguably, as the most effective movement in inflecting changes in many aspects of life, including politics. The aim, and to some degree the result, was to replace an understanding of art based merely on contemplation and sensuous pleasure with an understanding of art as action. Bru traces the engagement of aesthetics and politics initiated by the writings of Filippo Marinetti as they evolved in conjunction with Benito Mussolini's political aims for the Italian state. A central concern in this essay is to address the following question: What is the outcome when practical politics is understood as a form of artistic practice? John Bowlt examines constructivism in 1920s Russia which proposed to replace painting and sculpture with abstract and machine‐influenced modernist art. The artists of this period preferred photography, film, and industrial design as the means to creating art suitable for the new ideology of dialectical materialism. Bowlt portrays the tensions between the differing interests of artists focused on aesthetic experiments and the everyday life interests of proletarian culture that eventually contributed to the diminishment of constructivist influence. This tension between the artists and the needs of the proletarian society, as well as the shift to the right in the Russian state, thus diminished the constructivists’ hopes for changing the direction of life as Soviet leaders empowered a different model for the future of Russian society. Raymond Spiteri's “Surrealism as Aesthetic Revolution” explores the question of how surrealism's relation to politics can be understood over against its established role as a notable art and literary movement. This essay contrasts the views of Walter Benjamin, Pierre Naville, André Breton, and Louis Aragon in an effort to clarify both the political role of surrealism and its limitations as a political force. A second essay by Spiteri, “From Unitary Urbanism to the Society of the Spectacle,” traces the revolutionary efforts of the Situationist International (SI). This movement differed from the previous avant‐garde movements in that its focus was mainly on active revolutionary engagement within everyday life rather than through art itself. SI advocated the abolition of politics and served as a critique of other revolutionary political groups. The three remaining essays focus on the avant‐garde aesthetic revolution in particular geographic locations: Tyrus Miller, the United States of the 1960s; David Craven, Latin America; and Miško Šuvaković, Slovenia. Miller argues that artists, including popular artists in the United States during the 1960s, were informed by a “revolutionary social imaginary” which facilitated actions of protest. The resulting protests constituted a form of cultural revolution expressed in the actions of a counterculture with diverse interests. These interests clustered around such issues as anti‐war sentiment, civil rights, multiculturalism, and gender issues. The period marked notable changes in the arts—fostering artistic as well as aesthetic revolution—that were reflected in advances in areas such as civil rights and opposition to particular war efforts. Craven's essay examines the well‐known revolutionary protest art of Mexican artists including Diego Rivera and José Clemente Orozco as well as the lesser known revolutionary participation of artists, such as Alejandro Canales, in Nicaragua. According to Craven, both the Mexican and the Nicaraguan mural artists participated in aesthetic avant‐garde practices. Craven argues that the muralists, both in Mexico and in Nicaragua, were engaged in revolutionary protest aimed at the future—and sufficiently so—such that they qualify as aesthetic avant‐garde revolutionary movements. Šuvaković considers the role of the NSK (Neue Slowenische Kunst)—a network of Slovenian avant‐garde groups known for their artistic–political activism taking place in the post‐socialist culture of Slovenia. He argues that NSK exemplifies the role of aesthetic avant‐garde revolutionaries in facilitating the independence of Slovenia and that it acted in collusion with other post‐socialist efforts toward political change elsewhere in Eastern Europe during the 1980s. Among the NSK artist projects was their State in Time Passport, which was a project involving the conceptual creation of fictional state actions (i.e., the issuing of fictive passports) within an artistic frame and, in doing so, thus addressing the post‐socialist artistic and political concerns of the times. Erjavec excludes Dada from the aesthetic avant‐garde on the grounds that it lacks the requisite commitment to revolution. His arguments on this point are puzzling. To make this case it is necessary to dismiss the revolutionary actions of the Berlin Dadaists, which included revolutionary protests of the Dadaist artists Johannes Baader, Max Ernst, George Grosz, and others. Their art, and related activities, included responses to the political and social upheaval of the postwar era after World War I. Perhaps a closer look at the revolutionary aspects of Dadaist artists in Zurich, Paris, and New York would reveal a similar concern over the general state of the world even where there was not a specific program for the future. Perhaps it is necessary to recognize that the Dadaists were not necessarily all focused on the same interests. In this volume, Erjavec has assembled an informative selection of previously unpublished essays addressing both the well‐known aesthetic avant‐garde movements and less familiar ones. Each essay is bolstered with an extensive bibliography on the avant‐garde in general and in its specific forms. The text is illustrated with black and white images portraying major figures representing the respective aesthetic and revolutionary developments. Among these images are Russian constructivist Alexander Rodchenko's Suspended Construction, 1920; a still from Luis Buñuel's surrealist film L'Age d'Or, 1930; Diego Rivera's fresco mural Man, Controller of the Universe, 1934; a frame from Andy Warhol's Chelsea Girls, 1966; Asger Jorn's Situationist painting Paris by Night, 1959; and IRWIN's NSK mixed media The Enigma of Revolution, 1988. For the most part, the aesthetic avant‐garde revolutions cited in this volume address the societal disruptions and political realignments arising, in part, from fascism, capitalism, socialism, and post‐socialist solutions aimed at shaping the future of the world—or some part of it. The two world wars followed by controversial geographic realignments, with still unresolved consequences, have contributed to circumstances inviting new solutions. National revolutions in Latin America, China, and other parts of world have also provided opportunities for avant‐garde interventions aimed at shaping the future stages of civilization. By examining a range of aesthetic avant‐garde developments, Erjavec and his contributing authors both inform and raise important questions pertaining to the role of aesthetic avant‐garde projects. It seems, however, that these efforts exist mainly in short‐term duration and subsequently remain largely as concepts in art and cultural histories. Perhaps it is enough that such developments contribute to short‐term social or political changes in a particular nation or region. But it is less clear how the aesthetic avant‐gardes have succeeded in changing or becoming a part of everyday life experiences on a wider scale. It seems much easier to document actual changes in the practices of avant‐garde art itself than changes following from aesthetic avant‐garde social and political contributions. The essays offered in this volume will surely motivate our interest in exploring their topics further. The question left unresolved is this: Can any of the proposals of the aesthetic avant‐gardes examined here show lasting contributions toward changing the world? The essays in this volume illustrate the persistence and the scope of such efforts in the context of particular social and political developments over the past century. Less certain is how to measure the social and political outcomes of such efforts. We have the views of committed participants—but what about the effects in the broader world? And what exactly might be the role of the aesthetic avant‐garde in the future? A clue to this comes in Erjavec's introduction, where he suggests that the aesthetic avant‐garde of the future may be materialized in the world of discourse as opposed to change and transformation in actual historical projects (p. 16). In any event, the contributions of the aesthetic avant‐garde, as well as artistic avant‐garde developments, function in relation to other forms of cultural transitions. The dominant cultural transitions of our times, it seems, are informed by the shift from industrialization to electronic digital forms of civilization, worldwide urban growth, and globalization as well as revisions focused on racial tensions, human rights issues, and sexual and gender‐based social conventions. And all of these have contributed opportunities that invite avant‐garde responses into the future. With few exceptions, the concepts and practices that shape the world today come from scientific discovery, technological innovations, industrial practices, and enlightened political leadership. Perhaps it is wise to keep in mind that the role of the aesthetic avant‐garde and the artistic avant‐garde is to function in relation to these other developments. A more modest aim for the aesthetic avant‐garde forces might be, for example, as Harold Rugg reminds us in his essay “The Artist and the Great Transition,” to focus on aesthetic avant‐garde ideas as a contribution to self‐cultivation and the development of a personal philosophy of value‐driven living. To be sure, the contributions of the avant‐garde may serve as an essential part of education for those whose ideas will shape the artistic, scientific, technological, economic, and political landscapes of the future.

title: Teaching avant-garde practice as videographic research
abstract: As a practitioner of avant-garde filmmaking, my primary objective is to break the cinematic machine. As a found-footage filmmaker working in an academic setting, my goal is to critically plumb the textual depths of existing works through audiovisual production. My recent works include: A Movie by Jen Proctor (2010–12), a remake of Bruce Conner’s seminal found-footage work using YouTube and LiveLeak videos; So’s Nephew by Remes (thanx to Michael Snow) by Jorrie Penn Croft (2015), a remediation of an academic article about textual films made in the style of Michael Snow’s text-based opus So Is This; and Nothing a Little Soap and Water Can’t Fix (2017), a narrative mashup of scenes of women in bathtubs in popular films.1 Each of these works serves to illuminate, and critically comment on, formal and ideological functions of media apparatuses using the affective language of cinema itself. Rather than theorize or investigate the original works through the discursive format of the written word, I choose to draw upon the historical impulse of the avant garde to détourn – literally, to reroute or hijack – these texts as a means of levelling a critique against them using their own media language. Because my work hovers at a nexus of art and scholarly practice, it enjoys multiple venues for dissemination: film festivals and online hosting, as well as academic conferences and scholarly journals. In many respects my work is not so different from certain trends in the still emerging form of the scholarly video essay (or, as some prefer, ‘videographic criticism’). As explained by [in]Transition: Journal of Videographic Film and Moving Image Studies, the leading venue for peer-reviewed work of this kind: Practitioners of these forms […] explore the ways in which digital technologies afford a new mode of carrying out and presenting film and moving image research. The full range of digital technologies now enables film and media scholars to write using the very materials that constitute their objects of study: moving images and sounds.2 The emergent form of videographic criticism extends traditional cinematic study into the realm of production practice, employing clips of visuals and sounds as illustration and evidence for theoretical claims and observations. While, perhaps, a scholar’s first impulse in constructing a video essay might involve something like a direct translation from the printed word to the moving image, complete with an explanatory voiceover directing our understanding of the underlying audiovisual passages, the revolutionary potential of a developing form lies in its ability to push boundaries and establish (or refuse to establish) new conventions. Many videographic scholars – and educators – have accordingly embraced formal experimentation, somewhat defiantly, as a means for discovery, invention and the production of new knowledge. Catherine Grant, a prolific video essayist and co-founder of [in]Transition, for instance, argues widely for the importance of play and of trial and error when working with the materials of film and video. Writing with Christian Keathley, she connects contemporary digital practice to Roland Barthes’s formal play: Describing his own experiments in writing, Roland Barthes wrote that he sought to replace the scholarly ‘labor of knowledge’ (straightforward analysis and interpretation) with the more pleasurable and poetical ‘labor of writing’, which we might also think of as akin to playing […] Videographic film studies has a special potential to show something about our relationship with our cinematic objects of study, for it enables us to explore and express, in a particularly compelling way, how we use these objects imaginatively in our inner lives; and it can also be used to present something sharable about those objects – some attained knowledge or understanding – however surprising its content or unusual its form.3 Elsewhere, Grant elaborates, ‘we cannot know completely in advance the processes and forms that will help produce new knowledge. We need to have a notion that what we do is not just research but it’s experimental.’4 Jason Mittell has similarly explored, both in his own work and in his pedagogical approach to videographic scholarship, the notion of ‘deformative criticism’, a mode developed by literary critics Lisa Samuels and Jerry McGann.5 In this experimental method of analysis, an existing work is ‘deformed’ through any variety of techniques to render the work strange, thereby uncovering an otherwise hidden meaning or thread. As an additional gesture towards the video essay as creative research, Mittell frames the deformative aspects of video essay in terms familiar to digital humanists: ‘Videographic criticism can loop the extremes of [the] spectrum between scientific quantification and artistic poeticization together, creating works that transform films and media into new objects that are both data-driven abstractions and aesthetically expressive’.6 Reflecting on the workshops on ‘Scholarship in Sound and Image’ that they led at Middlebury College in 2015, Mittell and Keathley advance the principle that ‘formal parameters lead to content discoveries [… that] will reveal something about your object that would be hard to discover through more typical analytical means’.7 Mark Sample, however, has gone a step further, proposing a ‘Deformed Humanities’ that is ‘born of broken, twisted things. And what is broken and twisted is also beautiful, and a bearer of knowledge.’8 The Deformed Humanities is a practice of play, of deconstruction, of dissection, of demolition – all for its own sake. Instead of restoring Humpty Dumpty after his fall, Sample’s Deformed Humanities calls for him to lie there, a cracked shell oozing yolk. He is broken. And he is beautiful. The smell, the colors, the flow, the texture, the mess. All of it, it is unavailable until we break things […] The deformed work is the end, not the means to the end.9 This method of analysis, of course, bears much in common with the radical and subversive traditions of the avant garde. The recognition of the value of oblique, implicit and formally driven knowledge in video production by videographic scholars, together with an emphasis on the possibilities of poetic and lyrical expression as a pathway to knowledge generation, opens up rich and significant avenues for teaching film and media studies in a way that bridges theory and practice through active and experiential learning. Deformative and experimental approaches to the video essay clearly fit into a tradition of appropriative avant-garde filmmaking, which itself feeds into contemporary practices of remix and mashup. Drawing from the avant garde as both a critical and pedagogical tool taps into the resistant impulses of experimental filmmakers and artists, especially those working to dismantle and destabilize the ideological structures of existing texts; the techniques of subversion employed by found-footage filmmakers and remix artists are almost innately critical of media, even if such aims might not be explicit. If, as Mittell and Keathley suggest, ‘analysis must always be conducted, to some extent, on the object’s terms: that is, using its material – moving images and sounds’,10 then the implementation of avant-garde techniques that found-footage filmmaker Craig Baldwin calls ‘media jiujitsu’ engages media on its own terms. Media jiujitsu, or ‘using the weight of the enemy against itself’, involves re-assembling media objects in a way that self-reflexively refutes the message of the original work using its own audiovisual logic.11 This is not to say that the relationship to an object of criticism must be a combative one, but that the avant garde’s sceptical, resistant or mischievous approach to dissecting a media work can lead to fruitful discoveries. Dada, Surrealism, the Situationists, Fluxus, culture jammers, mashup artists and their brethren have created much media mischief. Here I will outline a few approaches to production practice that can yield fruitful educational results for students (and scholars). Delineating or codifying techniques of avant-garde filmmaking might feel counter to the very enterprise of the avant garde, but as a pedagogical strategy, a handful of techniques drawn from the history of experimental film practice can jump-start student exploration and play in the process of working with found-footage material. At its most fundamental, the practice of making holds significant educational value. Although the rising movement to legitimize creative practice and practice-led research in the academy is beyond the scope of this essay,12 the benefits of doing and making to deepening learning and generating new knowledge are well established, though nonetheless often neglected in traditional film studies classes. David Kolb’s theory of experiential learning – a pedagogical approach widely applied in education across disciplines at all levels – particularly serves to fuse critical thinking and media production. Kolb’s approach emphasizes that learning occurs not just on an intellectual level, but through the practice of hands-on participation, stating that ‘Learning is the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience’.13 This assertion parallels many other observations about the necessity of doing as a part of learning, including Heidegger’s educational philosophy that we can only fully understand an object of study theoretically once we have ‘handled’ it materially,14 Donald Schön’s reflective practitioner approach that suggests ‘knowing is in the action’,15 or, appropriately, video essayists Adrian Martin and Cristina Alvarez Lopez’s observation that video-writing means that ‘action precedes thought’.16 In essence, making videographic work means learning not just to read the language of cinema but to speak and write it – to interrogate film by (re)making film. Avant-garde approaches to working with found footage in a scholarly context, then, involve deconstructing, destroying, rebuilding, deforming, reorganizing, decentring, erasing – essentially sculpting something unexpected out of the raw material of someone else’s creation – in order to better understand its parts and the relationships among them. It is a kind of creative, generative reverse-engineering. Thus students might employ remix (a re-edit of an existing source), mashup (editing together multiple sources to create surprising juxtapositions), speed manipulations, frame enlargements or splitscreen/spatial montage as a means of achieving some of these learning effects. They might, for instance, work to create a continuity edit across two different film sources, as my student Zahra Cawley did in a mashup of Aladdin (Ron Clements and John Musker, 1992) and Mulan (Barry Cook and Tony Bancroft, 1998).17 She was exploring the notion of heteronormative representations in animated Disney films, to discover if she might deform those representations into a celebratory queer relationship between princesses Jasmine and Mulan. On one level her short work deploys a critique that demonstrates a strong theoretical understanding of the function of representation in cinema. But, on a micro-level, in order to make the sources convincingly converge through eyeline matches between the two characters, she had to carefully examine frame compositions and consider precisely how a single edit creates relationships across space and time – and in a way that is more conscious than instinctive, as can be the case when watching a film. The process of determining how two different sources can be edited together according to conventional principles of continuity editing is a deconstructive move, demanding that a student break the original works into disparate parts, examine the semiotic functions of those parts, and then determine how to create new meanings through juxtapositions using the very same semiotic rules. Once a student actively appropriates a formal device for new purposes, that device becomes tangible where it might previously have been invisible, enabling the student to see such gestures across other media artefacts and thereby make new kinds of connections. Other types of more methodical approaches to media manipulation can also prove surprisingly revelatory. Reflecting on their ‘Scholarship in Sound and Image’ workshops, Mittell and Keathley advance the principle that ‘formal parameters lead to content discoveries [… that] will reveal something about your object that would be hard to discover through more typical analytical means’.18 Mittell’s ‘equalized’ videos, for instance, in which he remaps the duration of each shot in a particular scene to the precise average length of all the film’s shots, work as an algorithmic method for altering the affective qualities of the original, with long, dramatic shots neutered in intensity and short cutaways extended to produce greater gravitas.19 Although the algorithm is mathematical, the effects are to a large degree left up to chance in the spirit of Dada or Fluxus, with useful implications for understanding the production of affect in a film through duration alone. Similarly, by editing together a particular motif from a large number of films (such as a ‘supercut’), students can produce a broader argument about the deployment of specific techniques or aesthetic choices that service particular media agendas. Modelling their projects on works such as Matthias Müller’s Home Stories (1990), which builds a suspenseful sequence using only moments of tension for female characters in melodramas of the 1950s and 1960s, Christian Marclay’s Telephones (1995), which sews together disparate conversations among characters on phones, or my own Nothing a Little Soap and Water Can’t Fix, which builds a critical narrative of cinematic representations solely from images of women in bathtubs, becomes the basis for new discoveries. Isolating a particular motif or device across a wide variety of sources teaches students about its systematic deployment, enabling them to see how it serves as a trope, convention or stereotype rather than a unique stylistic element particular to a single film. title: Art from Start to Finish: Jazz, Painting, Writing, and Other Improvisationsedited by becker, howard s., robert r.faulkner, and barbarakirshenblatt-gimblett
abstract: One guesses that it was sociologist Howard S. Becker, known for what is called “social reaction theory,” who had the major hand in pulling this collection together. (Robert R. Faulkner too is a sociologist, while Barbara Kirshenblatt‐Gimblett is a professor of performance studies.) Becker is the author of Art Worlds (University of California Press, 1982)—not a philosophy book, but containing data very useful for philosophical aesthetics about the actual workings of various artistic institutions and practices. The material in this volume orbits around two questions: what is the work of art? and, when is a work of art finished?—or, alternatively, what is it for an artwork to be finished? These questions are aired explicitly or implicitly in a group of fifteen pieces, which includes no less than four introductory texts, if we count Becker's own first chapter, “The Work Itself.” Before I turn to the general perspective of this book, let me address a few of the volume's superior contributions. Musicologist Paul Berliner's essay about Zimbabwean mbira music is a must‐read for any music ontologist who still wears European blinders. The mbira, or thumb piano, is played by plucking with both thumbs metal strips of different lengths attached to a resonating box. Its music constitutes a repertoire, but in a very different sense from that of European concert music. A performance of a “work” can last five minutes—or an hour—and need not observe obligatory structural points for beginnings and endings. Like Ghanaian drum music, performances are intrinsically social in character. Players learn how to stake out personal styles, but always within the context of a communal activity. Since players consider themselves both as preserving the tradition and as contributing to it, negotiations between members of the group are necessary. Striking differences from the European model of work‐performance are also profiled in Scott DeVeaux's essay, “This Is What I Do.” His subject—dear to this reviewer's heart—is the persistent attempt to convert jazz into finished works by recording them. DeVeaux regards this commercially motivated extra step as an inherently anti‐jazz project. Taking his theme from remarks by Sonny Rollins on the matter, DeVeaux believes that recordings are little more than advertisement for the living stuff. The one thing the essay could use to complete the story of this inherently paradoxical situation is emphasis of the ironic fact that it is almost entirely by recording that we have a jazz history. Faulkner's own essay on what in jazz is called “wood‐shedding,” or simply “shedding,” is also a gem. Although the term refers, over simply, to practicing, the jargon carries extra freight for jazz musicians. “Shedding” in jazz is ceaseless, but not in the bald sense that, like Artur Rubinstein or Jascha Heifetz, Dizzy Gillespie and Sonny Rollins never stopped practicing. Jazz practice is not practice for a finished work or for a finished performance thereof. The jazz musician occupies a place in a field of indeterminacy where only a fuzzy line connects discipline and imagination, planning and spontaneity. Thus, Faulkner's title, “Shedding Culture,” is a pun, which profiles the fact that the practicing jazz musician absorbs his culture in order (partly) to shed it. Unsurprisingly, Faulkner rejects the romantic story of jazz playing as sheer spontaneity. But he would presumably also reject the quieter myth that even the most adventurous jazz solo is a mere pastiche of learned material. The general picture is that the life of a jazz player is an ongoing work‐in‐endless‐process. One might want to qualify the claim by citing jazz subtypes, but Faulkner's piece has real depth. Artist Larry Kagan presents himself as a case of how artistic intentions can be radically revised along the way. Kagan began by shaping wiry bits of steel in forms that resembled drawings, for which he then constructed frames that would allow the wiry bits of steel to interact with the wall behind them. Because steel elements cast unanticipated shadows on the background, Kagan discovered that by not having a “one‐to‐one mapping between shadow and object, new object/shadow relationships become possible” (p. 167). Kagan thus found himself working with visual forms that went well beyond those with which he began. In spite of several striking pieces, this volume is overall a curious anthology. The editorial essays persistently stew over the question whether, given its methodological constraints, social science can “deal with the work itself.” It is never quite clear whether this question is about how sociology can address specific artworks or whether it is about whether sociology is able to cast some light on the concept of an individual artwork. Concern about either of these as apt questions for behavioral science would certainly be justified. But the methodology that would be relevant is made conspicuous by its total absence in this volume—analytic aesthetics. Too bad, because the questions that tumble down from the closet shelf throughout the volume are mainly conceptual ones, indeed, ontological ones. Some examples: Is a musical work the score—or perhaps the performance? Does a performance work have to be performed? Which is the “real work,” the plan for the work or the performance itself? The editors state that they “decided not to favor either” answer to this last question, but “rather to study how this question is decided in various areas of artwork” (pp. 5–6). But anyone looking for answers to any of these questions is going to be disappointed. Although contemporary analytical work on these issues abounds, virtually none of it makes an appearance in this volume. (Pierre‐Michel Menger's reference to Nelson Goodman is immediately overprinted by the conceptualizations of literary theorist Gérard Genette.) Of course, ontological questions about art forms cannot be undertaken a priori—as they might have been ages ago. Contemporary philosophy is vividly aware of the necessity of keeping conceptual analysis in touch with artistic practice. Although this volume contains data for philosophy, it nags at questions that, by the nature of the approach, cannot be sufficiently refined to become manageable, let alone answered. One gets the impression that the editors actually welcome their questions' apparent intractability, as when they state that the question of when a work of art is finished is “wonderfully open‐ended” (p. xiv). In fairness, the volume here and there does seem to acknowledge that none of the questions it tosses around have across‐the‐board answers. However, the overall trend of the book is to convert that point into some hazy generalities anyway. As a result, the nervous but high‐spirited skepticism that runs through the several editorial essays becomes fodder for a “convergence” on what the editors call “a common point of view” (p. xv). The spirit of the convergence is revealed by the editors' summary of the volume's aim—to address “art from start to a never‐reached finish” (p. 20, emphasis added). The volume's convergence seems to break down into four very general claims, none of which is convincingly argued for. First, an approach to art needs to be contextual. It is odd, then, that the contributors are unaware of the strongly contextualist trend of recent aesthetic theory. As it is, the volume is never quite clear about what context means or just why it is relevant. Second, no precise answer can be given to the question of when an artwork is finished. Menger's exposition of the manner in which Rodin endlessly tinkered with his works is presumably intended to support the case, since it shows how Rodin refused to play the conventional game of “now it's done.” But Menger admits that Rodin's approach was idiosyncratic. It cannot be generalized without hazard. Likewise, the important contributions of Berlin on Shona music and DeVeaux and Faulkner on jazz are contributions to specific artistic practices. Although we may not be able to attach any clear meaning to the idea of a finished jazz jam, there surely is a conventional way to tell when a performance of the Hammerklavier Sonata is finished—namely, when the last piano note dies away. Here and there in the volume, one finds apparent concessions to finishedness, but they are quickly overprinted by the main agenda. The contribution of Bruce Jackson fits the volume's “convergence” revealingly. Along with multiple versions of an anecdote from Jorge Luis Borges and a shaggy dog story about an undelivered James Joyce manuscript, Jackson stews up a hodgepodge of examples that he thinks makes finishedness totally problematic. (Sample: The fact that Max Brod ignored Franz Kafka's wish that his works be burned.) The editors consider the view of Barbara Herrnstein‐Smith's Poetic Closure that “artistic vocabularies” involve conventions—such as signing a painting—that signify “done.” But it becomes clear that they think we can safely ignore this useful proposal, except as grist for the skeptical mill and deprived of its ontological bite. The idea seems to be that conventionalism implies that the moment of completion is arbitrary and hence that, once again, unfinishedness rules. Of course, the ontological thrust of a conventionalist analysis taken seriously is that there is no hidden reality behind the convention. A third central theme in the volume is process. However, it is never clear what this entails. (Is it that there are no works, but only processes?) If so, it is striking that the philosopher of art as experiential process—John Dewey—is never mentioned. The fourth theme one finds in this volume is about contingency—the fact that artists face the constant, sometimes oppressive fact of choice. The matter is addressed from an economic perspective by Richard E. Caves, who wonders to what extent concepts such as expected utility can contribute to our understanding of an artist's practical reasoning as she or he works on a project. Should an artist at any point continue on a given project—or switch to another? How should we measure the utility of an artist's fanatical devotion to a project in spite of its seeming uncompletability? (Caves might have cited Zola's “L'Oeuvre,” the downbeat tale of artistic obsession carried to extremes.) True, because of the expected utility of the search itself, marginal costs can be turned into marginal benefits. Caves's (unsurprising) judgment is that economics cannot tell an artist whether to reckon marginal costs and benefits in market values or in subjective terms. For the editors of this volume, however, contingency seems to become an existential condition of the artistic process. Once pulled away from the agenda of the editors, the contribution of Larry Gross, titled “The Fragment Itself,” is not without interest. Beginning with Renaissance painter Giovanni Bellini, Gross traces a path toward a conception of the autonomous artist whose every gesture betokens genius. Eventually, etudes—including sketches, preparatory studies, and underpaintings—began to take on a value they never previously had. Grindingly switching gears, Gross cites de Kooning's infamous decorated toilet seat, asserting that it was art simply because of de Kooning's “choice.” Choice to do what?“To play a joke,” claimed Elaine de Kooning. And Arthur Danto has given the basic reason why the thing is not an artwork. It has no place in de Kooning's oeuvre. Michael D. Harris, an expert in African and African American art, notes how often the European appropriation of African cultural material has disregarded context. It is not clear, however, how his attempt to connect Yoruba art with the work of modern African‐American artist Juan Logan entirely avoids the problem. Other essays in the volume deserve even less attention. Becker's contribution takes a curious turn when he reveals that he abandoned what he intended to provide, namely a “sociological” analysis of Lester Young's recorded solo on “Lady Be Good” because he realized that this is not the kind of thing a sociologist can do. Stunningly, he declares that the musicologists whose work he cites are doing sociology anyway. The title of hypertext expert Michael Joyce's essay, “How do I know I am Finnish?” is presumably intended as intellectual wit—meaning that he is never finished. The piece reads like a rambling cross‐referencing letter to friends. In an interview, New Zealand artist Max Gimblett provides only a Dada response to the question of when a work is finished: “To begin,” he says, “is to complete. On the other hand,” he adds, “the completion is the front door” (p. 177). It is a pity that essays of the quality of Berliner, DeVeaux, and others do not find themselves alongside equally distinguished company in this volume.

title: Target With Four Faces (1955) by Jasper Johns (b. 1930)
abstract: Artistic invention, like scientific discovery, is a highly personal matter. Until the 20th century, artists' names were rarely linked in pairs during their lifetimes except as oppositional forces: Leonardo and Michelangelo or Matisse and Picasso, out of eminence and personal competition, Ingres and Delacroix, because they represented different artistic tenors (ie, Classicism vs the Romantic) or, like Jackson Pollock and Willem de Kooning, spearheaded 2 sides of the same artistic movement. Whenever I look at “Target With Four Faces” by Jasper Johns (b. 1930), I can't help thinking of his artistic soul mate and sometime lover Robert Rauschenberg (1925-2008). Like Braque and Picasso, who lived together in the same cold-water flat when they discovered Cubism, or the more recent pair of Gerhard Richter and Sigmar Polke, who did exhibitions together when they revitalized post-Modern painting, Johns and Rauschenberg are a historical dyad and, like the others, drifted somewhat apart with age. Leo Castelli, the most influential American art dealer of the twentieth century, liked to describe his discovery of Johns as an “epiphany”-more like an awkward moment. As the oft-told tale is once more reprised by Cohen-Solal in her masterful biography of Castelli, the dealer's request for ice in his drink led to the critical moment.1 Both Johns and Rauschenberg had their loft studios in the same building on Pearl Street in New York. Castelli had come to the building to visit the more established Rauschenberg with the express intention of possibly adding him to his initial stable of artists. Rauschenberg offered some refreshment and when Castelli requested ice for his drink, the artist said that he had to go downstairs to his neighbor because Jasper Johns had the one refrigerator they both shared! Castelli had already seen a Green Target by Johns in a group show at the Jewish Museum and had told several people how impressed he had been. Unbidden, he followed Rauschenberg down the stairs, entered Johns' studio, found it filled with strange but compelling paintings of Targets, Numbers, Flags and Maps, and immediately offered Johns the first solo show at his new gallery instead of Rauschenberg! Johns was 27 years old; Rauschenberg had been his mentor and his sometime lover. A year or 2 later, Rauschenberg also became a Castelli artist and the 2 young Southerners were launched on parallel careers that would revolutionize contemporary art; they were the bridge between the paint-handling of Abstract Expressionism and the subject matter of Pop.Figure: Caption Not Available.Jasper Johns was born in Augusta, Georgia, and grew up in Allendale and a variety of other small towns in South Carolina. He speaks and writes in short epigrammatic phrases and has never lost something of the shyness and reticence of his upbringing. His art shares those qualities. He left college for New York after only 3 semesters and is largely self-taught; this is quite astonishing given the beauty of his painted surfaces and his mastery of a variety of artistic mediums (he is one of the world's greatest printmakers). After being drafted into the Army in 1951, he spent 6 months on active duty in Japan, a cultural influence that undoubtedly resonates in the quietude and repetitive nature of his almost Japanese artistic practice and rich but monastic lifestyle. He returned to New York in 1953, and early the following year met the slightly older Texan, Robert Rauschenberg. It is difficult to know how much Johns learned from his friend during their 6 years of close association; outside the studio they even worked together on department store window displays. Among several other distinguished teachers, Rauschenberg had studied at Black Mountain College with Josef Albers, a great artist and famous Bauhaus pedagogue. Rauschenberg's outgoing nature, competitive spirit and technical knowledge must have spurred on his younger friend's artistic development. Significantly, Johns destroyed all of his art prior to 1954. “Target With Four Faces” (1955, Museum of Modern Art) comes from his earliest surviving work. Johns was much influenced by another friend, the composer John Cage, his meetings with Duchamp, and his readings in the philosophy of Ludwig Wittgenstein, 3 associations that you would predict from the nature of his work. After the important paintings of the 1950s and 1960s, Johns turned to abstraction in the 1970s and the subject of the artist's studio in the 1980s. For the rest of his career, images from the paintings are recycled in wonderful ink drawings on mylar and tossed back and forth between his paintings and prints in a variety of media, including etching and lithography. In his recent Catenary series, Johns has gone back to attaching objects, chiefly the aforementioned free-hanging curved string, to the surface of the painted canvas. The art of Jasper Johns has a natural reserve and decorum quite at variance with the raucousness of Rauschenberg and the heart-on-sleeve psychobiography of Abstract Expressionism. Nevertheless, there is an autographic quality to Johns' brushstroke that makes him everywhere present with an evident interest in revealing the processes, if not the meanings, of how and why he makes his art. Whereas the Abstract Expressionists saw themselves in competition with European painting, indeed had wanted to destroy it with their psychologically charged and completely non-referential wall-sized canvases, Johns and Rauschenberg sought to pour the real world back into art through the use of mundane symbols and everyday materials. Unlike the Pop artists and Minimalists who would follow them, the 2 young men, almost as a joke, retained the fleshy brushstroke of the abstractionists but squeezed the angst out. Most importantly, and more evidently in Johns, the paintings became more conceptual in nature, more like linguistic puzzles and less like voluptuous feasts for the eye; in this the 2 young artists were camp followers of their own Parisian hero, not Picasso, not Matisse, but Marcel Duchamp (1887-1968), alive and well and living in New York. By the time Johns and Rauschenberg sought him out, it was thought that Duchamp had given up art for chess. In truth he was secretly at work on his final masterpiece, Étant Donnés, a somewhat pornographic installation you can view through a peephole at the Philadelphia Museum, and periodically reissuing miniature copies of his previous greatest hits. Through Duchamp, Johns and Rauschenberg imbibed the spirit of Dada, the anti-art movement born in the ashes of the First World War: its mordant wit, its word play, its disdain for the nicely behaved painting. Johns looked at America in the 1950s and saw a country filled with symbols and objects capable of instantaneous recognition by the public (ie, the American Flag, targets, numbers, and maps) and realized he could turn the speed of communication against itself by frustrating the expectations of the viewer. For example, Johns often labels the colored areas in his paintings with the stenciled names of colors (eg, in a Map of the United States) except that the word “blue” is stenciled red in a white area. An American Flag painted by Jasper Johns exactly fits the borders of its canvas and has the same colors and same numbers of stars and stripes as its model. From a distance it looks like a real flag tacked to the wall; up close it has a lushly painted surface, its brushstrokes made more sculptural through the use of encaustic on paint-soaked paper glued to the canvas. Photograph it from a distance and it looks like a real flag, the symbol of our country; you can salute it but you can't run it up a flagpole, it's rigid and it can't wave. Is it a flag or not, a symbol of the country or a symbol of itself, or merely a painting of the symbol? Is it a sign for something else? The majority of Targets painted by Johns were like the Flags, instantly recognizable symbols that covered the entire canvas; of the early icons (targets, flags, numbers, maps) they are also his most abstract images. Since the canvas support wasn't round, these targets weren't like the ones hung in bars and used for playing darts but more like the targets used on a shooting range for pistol practice or archery. This lent them a slightly sinister air and the more valuable the paintings became the more dangerous the impulse to throw something at them. Sometimes Johns painted all the rings of the target the same color, green being a favorite for obvious symbolic reasons, and only the sculptural aspects of the painted surface gave a clue as to the location of the individual rings. Like the flag that couldn't wave, the painting became a target you couldn't shoot at or, like the Cheshire cat in Alice, one that almost completely disappeared when painted white. Like some apertures, Targets are pierced and share the property of roundness, as well as a variety of other meanings and associations, some born of the closeted life Johns and Rauschenberg led as homosexuals in the 1950s. Rauschenberg made this explicit in his famous painted object “Monogram” (1959, Moderna Museet, Stockholm), in which a real stuffed goat, a symbol for sexual randiness, has its mid-section encircled by a real rubber tire. And this at last brings us to “Target With Four Faces,” one of the first 2 Targets Johns painted, in which he attaches a wooden box with 4 small compartments and a hinged lid along the superior border of a target painted in blue and yellow against a red background. The medium is his favorite encaustic, a mixture of oil paint and melted wax, on a support of newsprint and cloth. The plaster casts are tinted to look like flesh but actually seem orange when seen against the wood, partially reflecting the red in the target. The resulting object, that word Minimalists like Judd and LeWitt would use for their constructions,2 is no longer purely a painting and not really a unified sculpture but something in between, a combination of both or even a divided self like the male artist who loves other men, their faces locked away in the little compartments or closets. In fact the 4 casts are from the same face, conceivably that of the artist hiding behind his art; the faces are partially obscured, almost wedged in, such that only the mouth and the lower part of the nose are visible. None of the eyes are visible. In her entry on Johns, Morgan says the hinged flap, which may be let down to completely hide the faces, “adds to the work's cryptic chill.”3 Steinberg contrasted the “impersonal stare of a bull's eye” with the blinded eyeless faces, and felt the anxiety of a dead world in which man-made signs, in the absence of men, became objects.4 In a further variation on this theme, “Target With Plaster Casts” (1955, ex coll. Leo Castelli), the companion painting to the present example, Johns inserted casts of an ear, a nipple, a nose, an eye and the male genitals, as well as other body parts, in 9 little boxes above another blue and yellow target on a red ground, and specified that it should always be exhibited with some of the doors to the boxes closed. It was Rauschenberg who pioneered the concept of 3-dimensional collages consisting of painted surfaces and objects taken from the real world; he called them Combines, of which “Monogram” is a prime example. In “Target With Four Faces,” Johns borrowed his method of working from Rauschenberg in much the same manner that Picasso took Cubism from Braque. The paintings of Jasper Johns caused an immediate sensation at their first exhibition; the Museum of Modern Art bought 3 works from the Castelli show in 1958, something it had never done with any other young artist. Art News, one of the most powerful journals of its day, placed “Target With Four Faces” on its cover. A number of soon-to-be-famous artists visited the first show; it proved a revelation to Frank Stella, then a student at Princeton University, who immediately started making object-like paintings out of stripes. As we have already seen, his work would be a determinative influence on the pioneering group of Minimalist object-makers.2 Kenneth Noland, one of the founders of Color Field painting, actually called his painted circles “Targets,” soaking his thinned paints into the canvas; these first appeared in 1959. The freedom “to act in the gap between life and art,” as Rauschenberg famously put it, inspired the Pop artists to give up the flashy brushstroke as well as the angst, and to use mundane subject matter from American advertising, the newspapers and the comic book. Warhol's printed and constructed “Brillo Box,” even more than the Flags and Targets of Johns, gave absolutely no visual clues as to how it differed from the real box containing real soap on the shelf of your neighborhood supermarket. To a significant degree, the Johns show signaled the beginning of the end for Abstract Expressionism's domination of the art world and the re-entry of recognizable subject matter into painting. Speaking specifically of his response to “Target With Four Faces” at the first Johns show, the eminent critic Leo Steinberg tried to explain his sudden sense of loss with the comment: “ … what really depressed me was what I felt these works were able to do to all other art. The pictures of de Kooning and Kline, it seemed to me, were suddenly tossed into one pot with Rembrandt and Giotto.” In other words, Abstract Expressionism was no longer a vanguard style but had passed into history, it meant the end of painting as a means of transformation or illusion, “so, the flat is flat and the solid is three-dimensional.”4 Many of the symbols and objects taken up by Johns and Warhol owe their visual power to excellent graphic design, an industrial process like others at the very heart of both Pop Art and Minimalism. And some of the visual power in targets and stripes, so useful in the construction of widely understood symbols, is undoubtedly owed their primacy in Nature's design of our visual fields. The Target very much resembles the concentric visual field of the retinal ganglion cell, first described by Stephen Kuffler.5 Pioneering electrophysiology of the retina by Nobelist Ragnar Granit had demonstrated that light could inhibit cells as well as stimulate them. The field of a retinal ganglion cell has a characteristic center/surround organization, most commonly “on” in the center and “off” in the periphery. It's thought that a stacked row of these retinal fields produces the characteristic bar-shaped field of preferred orientation for neurons in primary visual cortex. Painted targets create visual “pop” and after-images, they can glow with nostalgia or be used with historical irony. For a variety of non-optical reasons, then, Targets have remained popular subjects in art. Much like compositions written by Tchaikovsky, Rachmaninov and Stravinsky and based on melodies taken from Mozart, Paganini and Pergolesi, a number of young artists today (Ugo Rondinone, for example) continue to make targets, each a conceptual variation on an original theme by Jasper Johns. This freedom “to make something, change it, and do it again” as Johns famously and enigmatically put it, even more than his direct influence on both Pop Art and Minimalism, is part of his legacy and makes him one of the most influential artistic giants of the last half century. Michael Salcman, MD Baltimore, Maryland

title: “Phil” (1969) by Chuck Close (b. 1940)
abstract: MICHAEL SALCMANserved as chairman of neurosurgery at the University of Maryland and president of the Contemporary Museum in Baltimore. As art critic and neuroscientist he writes and lectures on art and the brain; see him on The Knowledge Network of The New York Times. As a poet his work appears widely: Alaska uarterly Review, Harvard Review, Hopkins Review, New Letters, Ontario Review, Raritan, and New York Quarterly; collections include The Clock Made of Confetti (Orchises, 2007), nominated for The Poets1 Prize and a finalist for The Towson University Prize in Literature, and The Enemy of Good Is Better (Orchises, 2011).The human face is the most expressive mechanism for meta-communication in our environment; we read the face for recognition and understanding, in joy and sadness, in the home and in the theater stall. That which is said or thought is not believed unless the speaker's face registers a congruent emotion. We decorate our faces to emphasize fierceness in war and attractiveness in love. By analyzing subtle structural similarities in familiar faces, we recognize children and grand children and certify membership in our kinship or tribe. Little wonder that the artistic portrayal of faces is one of the oldest forms of art making. From ancient Greece and China to the Renaissance in Italy and down to the present day, portraiture has been a sub-genre of painting and sculpture. Portraits of rulers and gods in stone, metal, plaster and crystal in ancient Egypt were highly stylized profiles; unique personality and facial features first appeared during the reign of Akhenaten in the 14th century BCE. The 3300-year-old painted limestone Bust of Nefertiti (c. 1345 BCE) in Berlin's Neues Museum is one of the most famous examples. From ancient Greece, similarly realistic sculpted heads and coins of leading rulers and personalities survive, including representations of Alexander the Great and Socrates. According to literary evidence, the lost paintings of Greece possessed a similar verisimilitude. The Chinese portrait tradition goes back at least a thousand years BCE but the oldest surviving paintings, such as the Court Portrait of Emperor Shenzong of Song (c. 1067-1085, National Palace Museum, Taipei) come from about 1000 CE. Many Roman portrait busts survive but paintings from that period are rare, except for a few frescos and the marvelous full-face portraits used as funeral panels in the Fayum district of Egypt (2nd to 4th century CE). The first major decline in accurate portraiture occurred during the Middle Ages when realistic likenesses of religious donors and rulers became relatively uncommon. Notable exceptions include the early self-portrait by history's first great composer, the mystic polymath Hildegard of Bingen (1152) and the secular portrait of Charles IV by Master Theodoric in Prague (c. 1360-1380). The great turning point in the history of the portrait occurred during the Renaissance, both in Italy and in the North, when artists rediscovered the art of ancient cultures and attention turned to secular, humanistic subjects such as the human body. Change in philosophic and societal norms was accompanied by a variety of technical advances including anatomical dissection, the perfection of single-point perspective and the invention of oil-based paint. Willem de Kooning, the American Abstract Expressionist, famously said that oil paint was invented for the depiction of flesh. In fact, the reputed inventor of oil painting, Jan van Eyck (c. 1395-1445), was himself a great portraitist. Van Eyck's pioneering work was deepened and enlarged by virtually every important artist who followed him: in the North by Cranach, Durer and Holbein, in the South by Leonardo, Raphael and Titian. For the first time it was possible to form some estimate of the character of a person by studying their portrait. The world's most famous painting, Leonardo's Mona Lisa, is a portrait, Las Meninas by Velázquez is a group portrait and fully 10% of Rembrandt's paintings are self-portraits. From the Baroque and Rococo (van Dyck, Rubens, Velázquez), to English and American painters of the 18th century (Gainsborough, Reynolds, Copley, Stuart), and the Neo-Classical, Romantic and Realist artists of the 19th century (David, Ingres, Goya, Delacroix, Courbet) portraiture has thrived. The Philadelphian Thomas Eakins ranks among the greatest portrait artists since Rembrandt; surgeons and scientists are the subjects of many of his finest works.1 John Singer Sargent and Whistler were also exceptional portrait painters. Among the French Impressionists and Post-Impressionists, Manet, Renoir, Degas and Cézanne were expert and enthusiastic portraitists, often picturing one another. Vincent van Gogh, a sensitive Dutchman like Rembrandt before him, similarly devoted 10% of his paintings to self-portraits documenting every stage of his life. Although the development of photography in the early 19th century sharply reduced the need for painted likenesses, both Eakins and Degas were enthusiastic about the new medium and used it to help shape and inform their paintings. In the 20th century, photography freed painting from a strictly reproductive function and important painted portraits incorporated distortions of color and structure for emotional or philosophical purposes. This was true of the Fauves (Matisse, Derain), the Cubists (Picasso, Gris), the German Expressionists (Otto Dix, Max Beckmann) and the artists who moved in Dada or Surrealist circles (Miró, Max Ernst and Picabia). With the rise of Abstract Expressionism in the 1940s, portraiture by major artists dropped off for the first time since the Middle Ages. Their art and that of the Minimalists was so anti-realist that no portraits were thought possible. In the 1960s, only the Pop artists, primarily Andy Warhol and Jim Dine, created a substantial number of drawings and paintings devoted to the human face. The few artists who continued to paint recognizable portraits, like the realists Alice Neal, Fairfield Porter, Alex Katz and Philip Pearlstein, were considered “old fashioned” and marginalized by critics and art historians. Despite the work of Francis Bacon and Lucien Freud in London, it did not seem that a type of contemporary portraiture could be built on the same conceptual principles as Minimalism and Post-Minimalism.CHUCK CLOSE, b. 1940, Phil, 1969.Synthetic polymer on canvas, 108 1/4 x 84 x 2 3/4in. (275 × 213.4 × 7 cm). Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; purchase, with funds from Mrs. Robert M. Benjamin 69.102. © Chuck Close, courtesy The Pace Gallery. Photo by: Ellen Page Wilson/Courtesy The Pace Gallery.Into this void stepped Chuck Close (b. 1940), a member of the most distinguished graduate class in the history of any American art school. Charles Thomas Close was born in Monroe Washington and studied at the University of Washington in Seattle (1962) before obtaining his M.F.A. at Yale (1964). His friends in New Haven included 2 of the most significant Minimalist painters, Robert Mangold and Brice Marden, and a classmate, Richard Serra, arguably the most important Post-Minimalist sculptor. Surrounded by budding conceptualists and minimalists, Close was known for his brushwork and described himself at that time as a “junior” abstract expressionist. In 1966 he abandoned expressionism and started painting from photographs. Given his educational background the decision to become a portrait painter must have seemed perverse. After living in Europe and teaching in Massachusetts, he made the choice, in 1967, to make things even harder for himself by renouncing his facility with the paintbrush and forcing an artistic breakthrough. As Close later said, “I threw away my tools, I chose to do things I had no facility with. The choice not to do something is in a funny way more positive than the choice to do something. If you impose a limit to not do something you've done before, it will push you to where you've never gone before.”2 At first, Close was considered a conventional photo-realist and his work was linked to that of painters like Richard Estes or Audrey Flack, artists who projected photographs onto the canvas and who, with meticulous technique, turned their paintings into believable simulacra of the original transparencies. The comparison of his work with theirs was easily made but facile and superficial. Close did not project slides but used a modular grid, did not use color but painted in black and white, did not use brushes but a spray gun and, in order to counter the machine-like impersonality of the process, restricted himself to monumental portraits. The subject matter of the other “photo-realists” was almost always limited to inanimate objects: shiny cosmetic cases on a vanity (Audrey Flack), automobiles (Ralph Goings), reflective storefronts (Richard Estes), pinball machines (Charles Bell) and street signs (Robert Cottingham). Moreover, Close, in giving up his paintbrushes and thick luxurious paint, became a serious photographer who preferred shooting his friends with a large-format camera and black and white film. In recent years he has even started making Daguerreotypes. Close began his first paintings by tightly gridding a normal-sized photograph he had taken and then gridding a similarly sectioned (enormous) canvas in a ratio of 1 to 10. By graphing the photo and the canvas in strict proportion to one another he was ready to transfer all of the information contained in the photographic image to the ¼” squares of the painting. In this laborious cellular method, Close did not project his photograph on the canvas. The process was so accurate that he could tape off all of the adjacent cells on the canvas and do one at a time; it would still come out perfectly. The canvas might contain 1000 squares but Close would need only a few drops of paint and several months to create the transfer. Each cell within the grid received a spray of paint in a single average tonal value (ie, from black or very dark through grays or whites) that matched the one found in the corresponding cell of the gridded photograph. The technique echoed the dot screen matrix used by industrial printers to achieve tonal variations. Further manipulations of the paint by airbrush, rags, a razor blade, and an eraser mounted on a power drill were carried out until a perfect match was achieved. His first picture using this method was Big Self-Portrait (1968, Walker Art Center), 107.5 inches tall and 83.5 inches wide; it took him over 4 months to make and it is one of the least ingratiating self-portraits in the history of art. The 9-foot tall head of Chuck Close stares out at us through giant glasses, uncombed and unshaved, a cigarette drooping from the corner of his mouth, every pore and imperfection of his face intensely magnified. Thereafter, the inexpressive faces of his friends and himself, warts and all, blown up to gargantuan size, always seen from dead ahead (no profiles allowed) would comprise the sole subjects of his art! Within that narrow frame, Close has carried out an extraordinary exploration. Close had discovered an almost purely mechanical or machine-like way of creating a portrait. Except for the identity of his sitter, virtually every subsequent artistic decision was predetermined: the image taken from a gridded photograph, the modular method of applying the paint with an airbrush, the lack of color (en grisaille), the size and shape of the canvas (9-by-7 feet, vertical), the head, face and shoulders as sole subject, and the orientation of the sitter (face forward) were all part of a standardized process. Individual brushstrokes, ie, autographic evidence of the artist's hand, could not be seen and the surface of the painting was as flat as the surface of the source photograph. The use of arbitrary and repetitive rules completely divorced Close from the preceding generation of Abstract Expressionists and aligned him with the conceptual and minimal artists of his own time. Indeed, his mechanical way of working with the grid, a repetitive and identical form like the cube, recalls one of the fundamental organizing principles of Minimalism. As I have discussed elsewhere, the grid has been used as a tool to transfer pictures from small drawings to large surfaces since Renaissance times but only in the modern period did the grid itself become the subject of a painting or the shape of an object.3 Sol LeWitt's cellular structures and early drawings consisted entirely of 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional grids.4 Given the mathematical organizing principles of geometric shape and repetition, Judd's objects and LeWitt's structures could be fabricated from simple drawings or even written instructions supplied by the artist to workmen in a distant factory; the artist's hand was not necessary for realization of the object. For this reason, Conceptual art became a natural outgrowth of Minimalism and LeWitt famous for saying “the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.” For Close, the grid is both the painting's plan and the method by which he transfers spots of paint to the canvas, the artist working almost like an ink-jet printer, not to directly enlarge the image but to imitate the source photograph. In his first black and white paintings Close obscured the presence of the underlying grid; as his art matured, the grid became physically evident in the painted image. Given his mechanical way of working and the absence of visible brushstrokes, the early paintings of Close could, in theory, have been made by sending a photograph to a printer who would lithograph or silkscreen the image onto the canvas; in point of fact, the paintings derive some of their considerable power from our knowledge that a machine did not make these large, immaculate objects. Direct confrontation with impassive human faces larger than our bodies creates tremendous psychological impact; Close uses the size and scale of Minimalism to make the paintings rise up like ancient monoliths. The effect of his massive photo-based portraits is similar to that of a 6-foot tall iron cube (“Die”) by Tony Smith, a 10-element Judd stack or a giant plywood beam by Robert    our  of the  in which we are  and  our  to our own  The    us in the  of  the   of the sitter  at the same time we    by the scale of the face     Whitney  one of the first paintings in the original  of 7 black and white portraits Close painted   Big  is   to the  of his  at the time he made  After  to New  Close  became a member of the   the new generation of artists,   and  that would  the art  away from Pop and  a more  and conceptual  Many of   as artist's  including   the  and   the  Richard Serra,   and  at  was   to  the    that would make him   were  to  and    as art  Chuck Close,  over 6-foot  and another   the  Philip  a    from Baltimore.
